title: The Sorcerer’s Apprentice (L’apprenti sorcier)
hook: An apprentice borrows his master’s spell, a broom comes to life, and nobody can make it stop.

painting.title: The Alchemist’s Experiment Takes Fire
painting.pairingNote: An experiment bursts out of control, glass flying and smoke rising, while the startled alchemist nearly falls off his chair; a mortar and pestle lie on the floor, the object that comes to life in the oldest version of the apprentice’s story.

facts: In 1797 Goethe wrote a ballad, “Der Zauberlehrling” (“The Sorcerer’s Apprentice”). An old sorcerer goes out; his apprentice, tired of carrying water, uses a spell he has overheard to make a broom fetch it. He has forgotten the word that stops it. The house floods, he splits the broom with an axe, and now two brooms carry water, twice as fast, until the master comes back and breaks the spell. The story is much older: around AD 150 the Greek writer Lucian told it with a pestle instead of a broom.

Paul Dukas wrote his piece exactly a century after the poem and called it a [[scherzo|scherzo]] “after a ballad by Goethe”. He conducted the first performance himself, in Paris on 18 May 1897, at a concert of the Société Nationale de Musique. It was customary to print Goethe’s poem in the score.

It is [[programme-music|programme music]] that follows the poem closely, event by event. You do not need the words: the bassoons play the broom, the brass the magic, and the orchestra the rising water.
It became by far Dukas’s best-known work, and its popularity came to irritate him. In 1940 Walt Disney used it in *Fantasia*, with Leopold Stokowski conducting and Mickey Mouse as the apprentice.
bigPicture.inOneLine: the silent workshop, the spell, the broom at work, the flood, the axe, two brooms and a worse flood, the master’s return.

movements.heading: Assez lent – Vif – Assez lent
movements.summary: One movement that tells the story in order. A slow, mysterious introduction sets the scene and hints at every tune to come. Then the spell, and the broom starts to walk, in the bassoons. The tune is passed around the orchestra and grows louder and wilder until the axe falls. A short silence, the pieces start moving again, and the second flood is bigger than the first. The master’s command cuts it off, the opening music returns, and four quick blows end the piece.

mainIdeas.name: The broom
mainIdeas.description: a perky, rather clumsy tune in short, detached notes, first in the bassoons over plucked strings. It climbs a few steps and keeps hammering the home note.

mainIdeas.name: The apprentice
mainIdeas.description: a lighter, eager tune in the woodwinds, decorated with quick grace notes.

mainIdeas.name: The spell
mainIdeas.description: a loud call in dotted rhythm for the brass, played with mutes, so that it snarls.

stops.hear: Hushed, high strings play slow, shifting chords; a flute adds a faint glint
stops.happening: The sorcerer’s workshop, still and mysterious. The introduction

stops.hear: A clarinet, then an oboe and a flute, quietly sing a slow tune
stops.happening: The broom’s tune, not yet awake, heard in slow motion

stops.hear: A sudden flurry of quick woodwind notes, which dies away at once
stops.happening: A first glimpse of the fast music to come: the apprentice’s impatience

stops.hear: Muted trumpets and horns blare a short, loud call in a jerky rhythm
stops.happening: The spell. The apprentice tries his master’s magic

stops.hear: A pause; then low instruments grunt and stir, and the timpani taps
stops.happening: The broom starts to move, hesitantly

stops.hear: The bassoons play a perky tune in short, bouncing notes, over plucked strings
stops.happening: The broom’s tune, now at full speed: it walks to the river and back with its buckets. The main section, *Vif*

stops.hear: The tune moves from instrument to instrument; harp and strings splash, the glockenspiel sparkles
stops.happening: The broom keeps working; the water starts to rise

stops.hear: A lighter tune in the woodwinds, with little grace notes, over plucked strings
stops.happening: The apprentice’s own tune: pleased with himself, at first

stops.hear: The brass call comes back, louder; the music grows faster and fuller, the broom’s tune now in the trumpets and horns
stops.happening: Too much water. The apprentice cannot remember the word to stop it

stops.hear: Two violent chords from the whole orchestra, then silence
stops.happening: The apprentice splits the broom with an axe

stops.hear: Very quietly, broken scraps of the tune in the lowest woodwinds, bassoon and bass clarinet, slowly fitting together
stops.happening: The two halves come back to life

stops.hear: The tune returns in two voices at once and builds to a far louder, wilder climax, with the whole brass section
stops.happening: Two brooms, twice as fast: the flood

stops.hear: The brass call rings out once more at full strength; the music stops in its tracks
stops.happening: The master returns and breaks the spell

stops.hear: The slow, hushed music of the opening; a solo viola sings the apprentice’s tune, sadly
stops.happening: Calm returns. The apprentice is sorry

stops.label: Last 10 seconds
stops.hear: Four quick, loud blows from the whole orchestra
stops.happening: The end. Some hear the master’s four smacks

notice: Follow the bassoons. In the opening minutes they are the broom, and their short, stubborn notes give it a personality: obedient, tireless and a little stupid.
Listen to the silence after the axe. Dukas lets it last long enough for you to think the trouble is over, and then the scraps of tune start to move again in the lowest instruments.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: James Levine recorded the piece with the Berlin Philharmonic in 1986, for an album with Saint-Saëns’s Organ Symphony; on the Spotify album it is track 5. Thirteen years later Levine conducted the new music for Disney’s *Fantasia 2000*, the sequel that kept Mickey Mouse’s *Sorcerer’s Apprentice* from the original film.

threads.title: A ballad without words
threads.body: Every event of Goethe’s poem has its sound: the spell in the brass, the broom in the bassoons, the water in the strings and harp, the axe as two chords and a silence.

threads.title: The same tune, wilder and wilder
threads.body: Almost the whole piece is built from the broom’s short tune. It begins slow and half-asleep in the introduction and is then repeated, louder, higher and in more instruments, until it fills the orchestra.

threads.title: A scherzo, a joke
threads.body: *Scherzo* means “joke” in Italian. The story is a warning, but Dukas tells it with a smile: clumsy bassoons, a glockenspiel, and four smacks at the end.
